narrative:
The model determined that you have an 80% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences, and both pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. While most accepted students placed around the middle of their class (roughly 6th out of 10), you ranked at the very bottom in both years. This low academic standing in law school was the main reason the model saw a high risk of bar exam failure.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 42, your score is noticeably higher than the average of 37 among accepted students, which gave the model some confidence you could still succeed. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

You should focus on improving your academic performance in law school if you retake courses or enroll elsewhere. Raising your class rank would have the biggest effect on future predictions. Consider seeking academic support, study coaching, or tutoring early in the program so that your grades better reflect your LSAT ability. With stronger in-school performance, your admission and bar exam prospects would improve significantly. (218 words)
